content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper introduces two approaches Diff-GAN and GAN-diff for TTS with the motivation to trade off diversity with quality. Specifically, Diff-GAN is a diffusion model whose denoising process is parametrized by conditional GANs and GAN-diff is a generative adversarial network whose forward process is constructed by multiple "denoising" steps.
content.strength_and_weaknesses: The paper aims to take advantage of both diffusion model and GANs.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: It is not clear why GAN-diff is called so at all i.e what is the diffusion part there.

Novelty: Paper has limited novelty: combining GANs with diffusion-like models.

content.summary_of_the_paper: A 2nd stage model is proposed in a 2step speech synthesis structure that combines diffusion and GAN.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
* Strength
  - Faster inference and better synthesis quality than the previous work (FastDiff). 

* Weakness
  - They trade off the strengths of the diffusion model, but not fast enough.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
* The authors omit the details of the comparative models. For each comparative model, the authors must specify which implementation was used and how it was trained.
I have serious doubts about the comparative samples presented by the authors. Taking the example of HiFi-GAN, which provides an official implementation and pre-trained model for easy comparison, there is a big difference in quality when comparing the samples presented by the authors with the audios synthesized by the official implementation and the pre-trained model. Since the model is deterministic, the quality should not be different if the same model was used. These observations make it difficult to trust the overall results presented by the authors.
If there is a pretrained model with the author's official implementation, it is preferable to use it to compare. If the comparison is made with non-converged models, the authors must conduct the experiments again and update the results.

* Moreover, it is easy to recognize that the samples of the models presented by the authors have quality-degrading artifacts and noise; it is also difficult to trust the results presented by the authors that these samples scored not significantly different from GT.

* The authors argue that GAN is difficult to learn and has a problem of easily falling into mode collapsing in general, not a specific model.
Ironically, the model proposed by the author has GAN added; it also has the disadvantages. If the authors claim that general GAN ​​problems do not occur in the method presented by the authors, theoretical background and experimental results on why this is the case are needed. In addition, the authors should analyze the phenomenons occurred in other models and present the results.

* The authors argue that:
"FastDiff 2 (GAN-Diff) breaks the one-shot forward of conditional GANs into several denoising diffusion steps in which each step is relatively simple to model, and thus it exhibits better training stability and mode coverage."
It is not clear whether training stability is better compared to FastDiff or better than other GAN models.
If it is claimed that the training stability is better than FastDiff, the theoretical backgrounds and evidences that the training stability of the DPM with GAN can be improved more than the pure DPMs should be presented. This is contrary to what the author argued about the problem of training stability of GANs.
If the authors claim that training stability is better than other GAN models, analysis results on training stability problems occurring in other GAN models are needed.
As far as I know, it is known that several GAN-based models used in the 2nd stage of speech synthesis are trained stably.
The authors claim "it exhibit better training stability," but no evidence to compare or confirm this has been presented for any model.

* The authors claim that:
"coverage degree does not distinctly impact audio quality. Inspired by these, we propose to trade off diversity for quality and speed by incorporating GANs into diffusion models,"
The method presented by the authors loses the strength of distribution coverage of the diffusion model, and the speed obtained through tradeoff is significantly slower than the GAN models, and it is difficult to say that the quality is good when referring to the presented samples.
If so, I would like to ask what this work is for.

* The authors claim that:
"it exhibits better training stability and mode coverage."
To support this, Section 3 seems to compare the diversity of the GAN and diffusion models. The comparison between the models designed by the authors is also meaningful, but the contribution of this paper can only be judged by presenting comparisons with previous works. GAN models have been improved in various ways, and it is difficult to find a phenomenon such as mode collapse in widely referenced GAN-based 2nd stage models. Comparisons between the models presented by the authors and GAN-based 2nd stage models is essential in order to agree with the authors' claim.

* There are a lot of duplicate expressions, and they will need to be corrected.
content.summary_of_the_review:
- There are arguments that are difficult to accept when based on the authors' claims and based on theoretical backgrounds.
- The authors' claims are difficult to accept due to the lack of theoretical backgrounds and scientific evidences.
- It is also difficult to trust the presented results.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper study GANs and diffusion models in the context of conditional speech synthesis. They observe that GANs produce high quality samples but do not cover the entire distribution. They show that diffusion models do have better distribution coverage but suffer from slow inference time, therefore they suggest to combine the two. The authors suggest two variants:
Diff-GAN - a diffusion model which uses conditional GANs to parameterize the de-noising distribution.
GAN-Diff - A conditional GAN where the forward pass is broken into serval diffusion steps.

They two variants present superior sample quality compared to FastDiff with a 4-iter sampling process (like in FastDiff).
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strength
The paper suggests a novel way to combine GANs and DDPMs to get the benefits from both of the generative model types. The authors provide experimental results which show superior results with a relatively good RTF score. The paper is written in high quality fashion.

### Weaknesses
The authors could have show the coverage distribution study (Figure 1) for the proposed method (maybe add to the appendix). Training of the GAN-Diff model is very complicated where you need a pre-trained FastDiff model to initialize the generator. The authors could spend a little more time to discuss the FastDiff model as it is a crucial part of the work.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is written in a high quality fashion, it's clear and well organized. It was missing some of the background on the original FastDiff method.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper is high quality and present nice results. It's also a first attempt to combine the GANs and DDPMs into a single model to get the benefits from both in a novel fashion.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This work proposes FastDiff 2, which introduces adversarial training to the diffusion model. Two methods were proposed (FastDiff 2 (Diff-GAN), FastDiff 2 (GAN-Diff)). FastDiff 2 (Diff-GAN) is based on denoising diffusion GAN and FastDiff 2 (GAN-Diff) is fine-tuned FastDiff model with adversarial loss. The authors argue that FastDiff 2 speed up the process of training and inference by reducing the number of iterations in DDPM. Experimental results show that FastDiff 2 outperforms FastDiff in terms of sample quality.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths

* Propose two methods (FastDiff 2 (Diff-GAN), FastDiff 2 (GAN-Diff)) to incorporate GAN into diffusion models for waveform synthesis
* FastDiff 2 reduces the number of Markov chains in diffusion models. (10s ~ 1000 steps → 4 steps)
* Explain how each evaluation metric was measured in detail.

Weaknesses

* The sample quality of Hifi-GAN in the demo page is quite poor than that of open-source Hifi-GAN [1]. The poor sample quality of other baseline models reduces the reliability of Table 2. It is necessary to explain which pre-trained model was used for each baseline model. 
* Both methods are not quite novel. 
1. FastDiff 2 (Diff-GAN): Denoising diffusion GAN [2] for the vocoder. FastDiff 2 (Diff-GAN) introduces the denoising diffusion GAN [1] for mel-to-waveform generation and the contributions of this work come from [2]. 

2. FastDiff 2 (GAN-Diff): Fine-tuning FastDiff w/ adversarial loss. 

2.1. This work argues that FastDiff 2 (GAN-Diff) makes adversarial training stable and better for mode coverage, but the experimental results do not show if the training of FastDiff 2 (GAN-Diff) is stable and brings sample diversity.

2.2. The training process of FastDiff 2 (GAN-Diff) does not have constraints for x_t to follow the pre-defined distribution. Thus, the fine-tuned model is no longer the diffusion that models the reverse process of the pre-defined forward process. It is necessary to show how each x_t changes at each timestep for FastDiff 2 (GAN-Diff) and whether it has training stability even after a lot of training iterations. 

2.3. This method requires the pre-trained FastDiff model.

* This work claimed that the proposed methods speed up the training process in a "principled" way by reducing the overall iteration to 4 steps, but didn't demonstrate the training cost of each model. Since reducing the overall iteration can increase the training cost required for each step, it is necessary to explain the training cost.
* In Table 1 and Figure 1, this work analyzed mode coverage & sampling speed in their own way for GAN-based and Diffusion-based vocoders, but they didn't show whether their proposed FastDiff 2 (GAN-Diff) and FastDiff 2 (Diff-GAN) cover the mode well in their own analysis. 
* Although FastDiff 2 (GAN-Diff) is a method of fine-tuning FastDiff, there is no explanation for the teacher model.

[1] https://jik876.github.io/hifi-gan-demo/

[2] Xiao et al., “Tackling the Generative Learning Trilemma with Denoising Diffusion GANs”
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
This paper is well written to understand. In terms of novelty, it is required to show more advantages of the proposed methods. The current version of the paper does not show the advantages in mode coverage or sample diversity compared to the GAN-based vocoder. Also, the sample quality of the proposed methods on the demo page [1] is not quite better than that of the GAN-based vocoder [2]. 
* Reproducibility - The number of training steps for each method was not detailed in the paper. 

[1] https://fastdiff2.github.io/

[2] https://jik876.github.io/hifi-gan-demo/

The poor sample quality of the GAN-based vocoders makes the results unreliable. It is required to show the advantages of the proposed methods. (Training cost, Mode coverage compared to GAN-based model, ..)

content.title: FastDiff 2: Dually Incorporating GANs into Diffusion Models for High-Quality Speech Synthesis
content.abstract: FastDiff, as a class of denoising probabilistic models, has recently achieved impressive performances in speech synthesis. It utilizes a noise predictor to learn a tight inference schedule for skipping denoising steps. Despite the successful speedup of FastDiff, there is still room for improvements, e.g., further optimizing the speed-quality trade-off and accelerating DDPMs training procedures. After analyzing GANs and diffusion models in conditional speech synthesis, we find that: GANs produce samples but do not cover the whole distribution, and the coverage degree does not distinctly impact audio quality. Inspired by these observations, we propose to trade off diversity for quality and speed by incorporating GANs into diffusion models, introducing two GAN-empowered modeling perspectives: (1) FastDiff 2 (Diff-GAN), whose denoising distribution is parametrized by conditional GANs; and (2) FastDiff 2 (GAN-Diff), in which the denoising model is treated as a generator in GAN for adversarial training. Unlike the acceleration methods based on skipping the denoising steps, FastDiff 2 provides a principled way to speed up both the training and inference processes. Experimental results demonstrate that both variants of FastDiff 2 enjoy an efficient 4-step sampling process as in FastDiff yet demonstrate a superior sample quality. Audio samples are available at https://FastDiff2.github.io/.
